Those are matters to which a committee might very wisely direct its attention. The advantages that might come from the publication of electoral contributions are apparent. I shall not detain the House at any greater length. I do not know whether these particular things that I have mentioned as being worthy of consideration are the most important but they strike me as being things that are worthy of serious consideration and things the consideration of which, even if they stood alone, would make it quite worth while that the committee asked for by the hon. gentleman should be granted. Following the proceeding adopted in 1906, I shall, with the hon. gentleman's consent, substitute for his motion a motion of my own looking to the appointment of a committee. In connection with that I notice that the hon. gentleman asks for a committee of nine. It is not quite clear to me that a com-

mittee of a smaller number might not be more effective. I do not want to insist upon it, but I think that the experience of .such things shows that when you have a small committee every member of it has a more realizing -sense of the necessity of his actively occupying himself with the duties of the committee than if you have a committee that is too large. In 1906 the committee which was appointed was a committee of five. I would be willing to adopt that number, or, if the hon. gentleman thinks that seven would be better, I would be willing to accept that number.
Seven.

The junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has brought to the attention of the House in a' very broad resolution a very important matter which ought to receive the attention of the people of Canada and which has excited the people of Canada during past years as the hon. member for Halifax very well knows. The different subjects which call for reform as regards electoral purity requiring the amendments of the electoral law are dealt with generally by the hon. member for Halifax within the four corners of his resolution. I would that the hon. member for Halifax had been able to show outside of the four corners of this resolution something of the spirit, something of the intensity of earnestness, which characterized a few of the remarks which he made to the House.
Amongst other things, the hon. member for Halifax, in the long speech which he delivered, outlined a woeful condition of electoral irregularity calling for a reform of the law in order to make more effective provision to punish bribery and fraud at elections, to ensure thorough publicity as to expenditures for political organization, to prevent the accumulation of funds for corrupt purposes and to prohibit all contributions whatever. I regret that I cannot, as I should like to, congratulate the hon. member for Halifax upon bringing these matters to the attention of the House in the way that he has done. I will be frank about it. I cannot congratulate him because I do not believe in his sincerity and if I did believe in his sincerity to-day I can only say that his sincerity to-day is of a very recent origin indeed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not permissible to question an hon. member's sincerity or to impute anything other than proper motives.

Well, then, I will say that the expression of my hon. friend, as contained in his speech and as contained	in the wording of this
resolution, is not consonant with the attitude, or the want of attitude, of my hon. friend in this House in the past. I am constrained to make these few remarks simply by reason of the fact that my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) has touched the crux of this whole question of electoral corruption, in the short speech he made, in which there was a great deal that might well appeal to the judgment of this House, and that is the want of sincerity in dealing with a matter so potent and so nearly affecting the rights of the people in order to secure the purity of elections.
My hon. friend from Halifax, amongst other things, asks expressly for a greater and more complete disclosure of election accounts by candidates and a disclosure of the contributions to political funds. My hon. friend sat in this House in the session of "1907-08, and he was a great admirer of the then able Minister of Justice, Sir Allen Aylesworth. When the Dominion Elections Act was introduced into this House, heralded by the Speech from the Throne in language almost word for word that of my hon. friend's resolution, and purporting to be aimed at preventing all these acts which are complained of, a resolution was offered to the House along the very same lines that my hon. friend's resolution now follows, and it was rejected by the then Minister of Justice, whom my hon. friend supported and with whom he agreed on that particular occasion without one word of dissent. More than that I find that the then Minister of Justice stated that he had never heard any complaint, such as was sat forth in the amendment moved by the then Opposition, which called for the strictest possible enforcement of the principle of disclosure in regard to contributions, the very thing that my hon. friend asks for now in this resolution. If I am permitted I will quote from ' Hansard ' of 1908, page 11,886:
My hon. friend from Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) warns to reiorm all that. He wants more particularity in several respects. He wants the vouching of accounts, the making of affidavits and the greatest fulness of minute details in the statements that are to be made out, supported by statutory declaration which are the equivalent of affidavits. He provides the candidate may not take his seat until these returns and declarations are made. He provides a penalty for failure on the part of the candidate to comply with the requirements of this section; also a special penalty in case

there be anything untrue in the declaration; and so on, through an elaborate set of sections, to provide for a condition of things in regard to which I have not heard at any time of any grievance existing under the system which has been so long in force in this country.
My hon. friend from Halifax sat in this House during that session when the electoral law .was under consideration for the best part of three months, and I have searched and searched in vain for one word spoken by the hon. gentleman for or against the proposed changes in that law. When that amendment, moved by the Conservative party then in opposition, and calculated to bring about a r,eform in the Elections Act, was negatived by the then Minister of Justice, the hon. gentleman supported his minister, or, at all events, never, during the whole of that session, raised his voice upon the subject of that Bill, or to protest against election corruption. I would that I could congratulate the hon. gentleman upon his sincerity; I would that I could believe he means all he says in his resolution. But I do congratulate him and those who sit with him upon a circumstance that will appeal to the better judgment of this country, and that is, that although the hon. member be not sincere, he has been met to-day, by the Minister of Justice, with a very much more cordial reception, and in much better faith, and with a much more evident desire to remedy the evil, than ever was extended by the Liberal Government to any mover of a resolution, having for its object the securing of purity in elections. I congratu late the Minister of Justice upon the course he has taken to-day, and I earnestly commend to him the consideration of the whole question from a generous point of view, having regard to the making of such changes in the electoral law as shall moderately, and at the same time firmly, provide for the removal of existing defects.
The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) spoke about making polling day a holiday; but he was Postmaster General in the late Government when my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Mac-donell) introduced a Bill to make election day a public holiday, and he entered no protest when that Bill was rejected by his government. These things go to show the insincerity of hon. gentlemen opposite in now displaying anxiety to remedy electoral corruption, when, notwithstanding that they were in power for fifteen years, they took no measures towards that end. These hon. gentlemen opposite, when in office, rejected every resolution which tended to 58J
reform, and they aggravated their rejection by the statement that they never heard of any such thing as political corruption existing in the country. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) says that these evils are of long standing in the country, but he made no protest in 1908 when the Minister of Justice in the Liberal Government declared that he never heard of them. According to the contention of my hon. friend, political corruption prevailed in 1908, and he came to this House in the general elections of that year, elections which under the Liberal Administration was bristling with irregularities and corruption,-but he kept silent on the subject.
I do hope that something will be done in consequence of the broad-minded action of the Government in leaving this question open for consideration by a committee, and I am satisfied that the action of the Government in this matter will meet with the approval and the plaudits of the people of the country.

It would have been surprising indeed if in this discussion we did not hear the tu quoque argument, which is the standard argument of gentlemen opposite.' Whenever any question of this kind is brought before the House, the answer of hon. gentlemen opposite is: We are no better than you are, and you are just as bad as we are. My hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) says that when he and his friends were in opposition they brought to the attention of the House the laxity of the electoral law such as it was then, and such as it is now, and that the Liberal Government failed to amend it.
Hear, hear.

' Hear, hear,' says my hon. friend; then why do you not amend the law, now that you have the power to do so? Tne Conservatives proclaimed that if they came into power they would remedy these evils, and indeed they made that one of the planks in their Halifax platform. This Government has been two years in office and nothing has been done. The Prime Minister was in favour of reforming the electoral law once he got into power, and I recall to his mind these words in the Halifax platform:
More effective provisions to punish bribery and fraud at elections, to ensure thorough publicity as to expenditures by political organizations, to prevent the accumulation of campaign funds for corrupt purposes and to prohibit contributions thereto by corporations, contractors and promoters, to expedite the

hearing of election petitions, to provide for a thorough investigation of corrupt practices, and, if necessary, to appoint an independent prosecuting officer charged with that duty, to simplify the procedure thereof, and to enforce the laws so amended.
If hon. gentlemen opposite question our sincerity, what are we to say of their sincerity when, although two years in office and having the responsibility of carrying out that programme on which they sought the support of the people, they have done nothing?
The only thing to the point in the speech of the Minister of Justice-a speech in which in some respects I would largely concur-is that, in his opinion, if the electoral law is not as satisfactory as it might be, it is because in some respects it is too severe. I think I heard him so express himself. So that even with the opinion of the Government to-day that the law is too severe, we are very far indeed from the position taken by my right hon. friend when he laid down the programme which he placed before the people at that date. It is no use bandying accusations from one side of the House to the other upon this question. Let us try to deal with it in a fair manner. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) *has to-day given us an example of moderation in the manner in which he has presented the question to the House. He has done it in a very moderate manner, more moderate than I perhaps might have expected. He has abstained from all recrimination, although the temptation might have been great to him to go into some matters in which he might have had a wide field to attack the party now in power. Instead of that, he has asked Parliament to throw aside all other considerations, and to approach the question simply from the point of view of formulating principles so as to deal with what is admittedly an evil. He has been moderate in his speech and moderate in his conclusions. After the statement in which he recalled the speech of my right hon. friend, he might well have called upon the Government to implement the promise which they made when they were soliciting the suffrages of the people. Instead of taking that position, he has simply taken the very moderate course of asking that the matter be investigated by a committee of the House so as to report what, if anything, is to be corrected. Certainly no more moderate course could have been pursued by my hon. friend, and I do not know if I had been in his place that I would have

been as moderate as he has been. Perhaps I would have been more tempted to call upon the Government to do what they have promised to do, and to bring on the legislation which they have promised.
Since my hon. friend has asked tire two parties in this House to lay aside all recrimination and to look upon the question in its broader aspect of the national honour and safety, I am disposed to follow along the same line. If we were to follow the bad example-if my hon. friend will permit me to speak my mind-which has just been given by my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr,. Boyce), I would not speak as I do now; but I think that my hon. friend on reflection will come to the conclusion that the speech' which he delivered was not called for or in keeping with the question now before the House.
Let us deal with the matter simply as it is. So far as corrupt practices in elections are concerned, I do not know that there are any gentlemen on the other side of the House who are in a position to cast stones at members on this side. There has been great temptation and I do not know that the party to which I belong is without sin in that respect. I do not wish to make any political capital out of this question; I rather approach it from a broad point of view, admitting that there are offences against the law; that the law is not so perfect as it ought to be, and that there is room for improvement.
When my right hon. friend the Prime Minister laid down his Halifax programme, he made with the public a very large contract, one rather greater than he is in a position to implement even now that he is Prime Minister. But there are some suggestions there that are worthy of consideration, and that the committee which may be appointed may well consider; amongst other things the advisability of ensuring thorough publicity as to expenditures by political organizations. The American people have adopted this system. The law of this country also at this moment provides to some extent for publicity as to expenditures; but in that, as in many other things, the law is a dead letter. What is the reason of that?' If we are to speak with absolute candour, I think I agree to a large extent with my hon. friend the Minister of Justice that the law to-day is too severe; but whilst it is too severe in some respects it is too lax in others. The law can be amended in these two respects, to lessen this severity and at the Same time to ameliorate the laxity which may exist.

I will give two cases in point. In controverted elections men have been unseated and disqualified for the most trivial offences. I remember a case of a young friend of mine who many years years ago was a member of this House, whose election was protested, and who was unseated and disqualified because he had paid the sum of $2 to a cabman for having taken him a certain distance, and the court thought that it was excessive. If that money had been paid outside of an election, nobody would have thought anything of it, and I do not believe it would have been questioned. The young man gave the $2 to the cabman perhaps because he had no coin in his pocket at the time. I am sure that he had no thought of corruption in his mind; but owing to the fact that it was during an election the judges were very severe upon him.
On the other hand, there have been cases in which, from the information which I have had, outrages of the most damnable character have been committed in the elections and nobody has been examined at all and no evidence offered. In the case I have in mind, the sitting member resigned his seat and the judges thereupon declared that they had no jurisdiction, and that therefore they would not go into those allegations. To-day the law is such that a man can be unseated for a trivial offence of which he may not have been personally cognizant in any way whatever; if done by his agent. On the other hand, another man who has been elected, simply through an abuse of the law, through corruption unlimited, can escape the consequences merely by resigning his seat, upon which the. court can say that it has no jurisdiction. In this respect the law can be amended and improved, and there is room for investigation. If the committee goes into its work as it should be gone into, simply to find what are the faults of the law and what are the appropriate remedies, I think it will do a good work; but I have my doubts as to the advisability of having a committee upon this question. The matter, however, has been decided upon. I hope that the committee will report during the present session, and that it will make a report upon which legislation can be based and action taken.
There are one or two suggestions which have been made as to which it might be just as well for me to give my views. My hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Boyce) a moment ago stated that the late Government had rejected an amendment of the
law to make the polling day a holiday. For my part I question very much the advisability or wisdom of making the polling day a holiday.
If you make election day a holiday, you will invite many offences against the law. We must not forget than when polling day comes, public opinion is often wrought up to an almost feverish point. If you make such a day a holiday and prevent people from working at their usual avocations, the temptations to disorder will be very great.
I believe, on the contrary, that polling day should be a working day as usual. But I should welcome a provision in the law that every man shall have an hour, or two hours, to record his vote. I know of cases, as everybody must, for these cases are not isolated, of working men being restrained from the exercise of their franchise, perhaps not actually prohibited, but impediments placed in their way. If the law should provide that every man could get from his employer at least an hour to record his vote,
I should welcome such a reform.
Then, as to compulsory voting:	I have
not very strong views on that point. I am far from being sure that compulsory voting would effect the reforms expected of it; at the same time I should not object to it if it were enacted in the law. Suffrage is not a right but a privilege, and if the voter does not choose to exercise the privilege, it is his own misfortune, and I do not know how you can remedy it. If you bring him to the poll I do not know that that will insure his having better judgment in the matter. There are circumstances, we all know, where men have conscientious scruples against exercising their voting privileges, having no sympathy with any of the candidates. I do not see how you can compel a man to vote against his conscience. But, it is said-bring him to the poll, even if he only casts a blank ballot. I think it would be better to leave it as it stands and let it be a matter of conscience for every man to vote as his judgment tells him.
But these questions are of little consequence and minor usefulness. The great thing is to prevent corruption and bribery in election. The hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) says that this country is awfully corrupt, that our offence in this respect is r'ank and smells to Heaven. I do not share that pessimistic view. I know that there is in every election some corruption. Unfortunately, it has been so ever since there were elections, and I am afraid that so it will continue. The most

that we can do is to remedy the evil so far as posssihle by providing punishment for curruption, and proper machinery for enforcing that punishment. We must recognize that the machinery we now have has been for some years almost dormant; election petitions have become almost a farce. I think that in this matter the Minister of Justice has a worthy field of operation, and should propose such amendments to the law as will make the Controverted Elections Act more effective than it has been in the past. That is the primary reform, in my judgment-to provide that the trial of elections shall be speedy, that they shall 'be based upon facts and not upon -general allegation of facts as at present, and when the facts are alleged, there should be a most thorough investigation.

speakeroldname: Eight Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I remember very well the occasion when I moved in this House a resolution very much along the lines of that proposed by my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean). Let me say at once, I find nothing in the manner in which my hon. friend has presented this matter to which I desire to take the slightest exception.
When I proposed a somewhat similar motion, I remember, gentlemen who at that time were members of the Government inquired of me, before the motion was to be reached, whether or not I proposed to take advantage of the occasion to engage in controversial discussion as to election corruption in the country. I told them that I had not the slightest intention of saying one word of a controversial character, as my object was to bring about some reform in the laws which, I thought then-and still think-desirable. The gentleman who was then Minister of Justice, now Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, told me that under the circumstances there would be no objection to the motion.	He informed
me that it was the	proposal of
the Government to introduce a resolution itself, whereupon I at once consented that my motion should be dropped and his take its place. That was done, but owing, if I remember well, to the fact that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick shortly afterwards became Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, and another succeeded him as minister, no action, so far as I recollect the matter, was taken upon the report of that committee.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has

alluded to some observations of the Minister of Justice (Mt. Doherty) and seems to conclude that the only object of the Government is to bring about a relaxation of the election law. I do not think my right hon. friend put that quite fairly. The, Minister of Justice, as I understood his observations, stated that in some respects the law as it exists at present oversteps itself, that it is not enforced for the Teason that it does not command the sympathy and support of public opinion. Laws of this character, like sumptuary laws, must depend on the respect and support which they obtain from public opinion throughout the country, and in any particular community in which they are invoked. It is not the desire or intention of the Government to relax the law, but to give to the country an election law which will be properly enforced.
My right hon. friend has alluded more particularly to the operation of the Controverted Elections Act, and I am entirely at one with him in the opinion that the committee might find very good scope for its activity in bringing about some reform in that respect. On more than one occasion in this House, and on the public platform as well, I have called attention to the very great expense, and especially the very great delay, involved in the operation of the Controverted Elections Act as it stands at present, and by reason of the interpretation placed by the courts upon certain provisions of that Act.
Owing to a decision, which I do not intend to criticise, made by the highest court in this country a good many years ago, we find ourselves confronted with this situation. A petitioner files a petition against a candidate at a particular election. It is immediately urged against him that, under section 271 of the Dominion Elections Act, he had not the right to vote, by reason of the fact that he had paid for the conveyance of some voter to the poll. The result is that the court, instead of proceeding to determine whether or not the candidate
i.s guilty of an infraction of the election law, occupies months, sometimes years, in determining whether or not the petitioner has been guilty of an infraction of the election law. That sounds like a story from .some comedy, but in the sober recital of legal proceedings in the various courts of Canada such instances will be found. As a matter of fact, I think the proceedings upon what are known as preliminary objections have obtained a scope and been

permitted an operation altogether beyond what was the intention of those who framed the statute in the first instance, and I hope that the labours of this committee may result in some improvement of the law in that regard.
My hon. friend the member for Bona-venture (Mr. Marcil) has alluded to the fact that candidates in this country are subject to the consequences of the actions not only of those whom they appoint as their agents, but of those who, within a certain construction placed upon their acts by the courts of the country, are deemed to be their agents, although they had no actual authority. It will be borne in mind that any person who actively works or canvasses for a candidate, although without his request but to his knowledge, becomes his agent and renders him responsible for the consequences of his acts to the extent of voiding the election. Some amelioration of the law was made in 1892 or 1893,
I think, when Sir John Thompson was Minister of Justice, in this respect:	If
the candidate could show that he had taken certain precautions to avoid the commission of offences by his agent, and if the improper acts committed by the agent were of a trivial character, the candidate might not be unseated. I would like to remind the House that the English law goes far beyond our own in that regard, because, if I remember correctly, an offence by a certain class of agents in Great Britain, although committed without the knowledge or consent of the candidate, renders the candidate, for the remainder of the parliamentary term, ineligible to sit in the House of Commons.
The hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) alluded to the importance of summary proceedings. If I am not mistaken, under the election law at the present time, summary proceedings can be taken against any person.
I do not think in that way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They can be taken, I think, before a magistrate. I speak with all deference to the hon. gentleman; I have not examined the question closely, but there is a provision in the Dominion ' Elections Act for the taking of summary proceedings against persons who are guilty of infractions of the law, and it is a very-common custom, in hotly contested elections, to have persons watching the proceedings in order that they might take the summary proceedings alluded to with the
least possible delay, and prevent any repetition of them. However, if there is any defect in the law in that regard, 1 certainly agree with the hon. member for Peterborough that it should be remedied.
The statute in regard to expenses, the provisions of which are contained in sections 263 and 264 of the Elections Act, goes pretty far if it is observed. I think most members of this House have been careful to observe it, but I would like to point out that those who do not observe it render themselves liable to a penalty of $20 for every day during which they fail to make the necessary declaration within the prescribed time. Further than that, any candidate who makes a statement of the expenses incurred in his election whicli to his personal knowledge is untrue, is guilty of an indictable offence. We will admit that those are fairly stringent provisions, but, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), the difficulty is that the law does not seem to be enforced in that regard as it should be.
I would like to say to the hon. member for Halifax that I investigated the English election law and its results very carefully some years ago, particularly at the time when I made the motion to which allusion has been made this afternoon, and I can say that there are difficulties in Great Britain just as there are in this country. In England the judges have had a good deal of difficulty in endeavouring to prevent evasions of the election law through what is known as the nursing of constituencies by means of payments, adroitly spread throughout the constituency, and effected in such a way that they do not come within the exact terms of the election law. We must all realize that no matter how stringent we make our election law in this country, fraud has manifold devices at its command, and we must, after all, depend tp a great extent on the force of public opinion. The subject of compulsory voting, which was alluded to by my right hon. friend, has been the subject of discussion in this House on more than one occasion. I recall that one of the committees made a report on the subject, in which it was suggested that any man having the right to vote, who did not exercise that right at a particular election should, unless he could show good cause to some court for having abstained from voting, lose his right to vote at the succeeding election. I agree with my right hon. friend that de-

vices of that kind would be very difficult to carry out in an effective way. I also agree with him that we are liable, per, haps, to exaggerate the extent to which actual bribery of the electorate is carried on. Personally I do not believe that it is carried on anything like the extent to which is represented in some quarters. Undoubtedly the offence of personation, particularly in large cities, is of very wide-spread extent, and the offence of conveying voters to the poll is one common not only to the city constituencies, but to all the electoral districts of Canada. There was grave question, when this subject was discussed here some ten years ago, as to whether the law should not be modified in that regard, because public opinion does not respect it very much. I remember very well that when a most worthy organization to enforce purity in elections was established in the Maritime provinces during the election campaign of 1908-and this organization performed excellent work

it did not attempt, if I remember correctly, to exercise any supervision over offences of that kind, because it did not consider that the law in that regard was sustained by public opinion. I realize fully the difficulty in that respect; on the one hand if you do not have some law governing cases of that kind you leave the door wide open for bribery of a , certain character and, on' the other hand, if you make provisions too stringent, you bring about a condition of affairs which public opinion does not respect. The suggestion made on a previous occasion was, if I remember correctly, to permit the conveyance of voters at an election under certain restrictions and subject to certain safeguards. Whether or not any change in the law in that regard could be advantageously brought about I do not know; that would be a matter for consideration by the committee.
I do not intend to enter into any controversial aspect of the subject, nor to deal with what has been alleged as to our supposed delay or neglect. If we had thought that a general election was so imminent as some of our friends on the other side seemed to think, we should have taken up the subject before; but we considered that reform would be brought about before the next general election. The subject has been under consideration for some time by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, and would have been brought forward at an early date in this session; but as my hon. friend the junior member

for Halifax had placed his motion upon the Order Paper at the very commencement of the session, it was thought desirable to give him an opportunity of bringing the subject under discussion upon his motion, rather than to intervene before that motion had been reached. I must apologize to the House for having trespassed a few minutes beyond the hour for recess. I move now that the debate be adjourned.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
At six o'clock the House adjourned with question put, pursuant to rule.
Thursday, February 19, 1914.
